title: Ancient astronauts: Sitchin's Anunnaki claim
summary: Author Zecharia Sitchin claimed that Anunnaki astronauts from a hidden planet genetically engineered Homo sapiens about 300,000 years ago to mine gold.
description: The ancient astronaut idea, popularised by Erich von Däniken's 'Chariots of the Gods?' (1968) and the television series 'Ancient Aliens', holds that extraterrestrials visited Earth in prehistory and shaped human biology and culture. Its most specific version comes from Zecharia Sitchin, whose 1976 book 'The 12th Planet' claimed that Sumerian texts describe the Anunnaki, beings from a planet called Nibiru on a 3,600-year orbit, who arrived about 450,000 years ago and created humans as labourers by modifying an existing hominin. Adherents also credit alien visitors with building or inspiring monuments such as the Egyptian pyramids and Puma Punku in Bolivia. The claim is placed here at Eridu, which Sumerian tradition associated with the god Enki, central to Sitchin's story.
mainstreamView: Assyriologists reject Sitchin's translations: in Sumerian and Akkadian texts the Anunnaki are gods, and nothing in them describes a planet Nibiru, space travel or genetic engineering. The fossil and genetic record shows Homo sapiens evolving gradually in Africa from earlier hominins, with no sign of an abrupt artificial origin, and no planet with a 3,600-year orbit has been found despite extensive sky surveys. Ancient monuments are well explained by archaeological evidence of the tools, quarries, workforces and building techniques of the people who made them.

title: Omo Kibish and Herto: early East African sapiens
summary: Fossils from Ethiopia's Omo valley, at least 233,000 years old, include Omo I, one of the oldest skulls with an essentially modern human shape.
description: A Kenyan expedition led by Richard Leakey recovered the Omo I and Omo II skulls from the Kibish Formation in southwestern Ethiopia in 1967. Long thought to be about 195,000 years old, Omo I was shown in 2022 to lie beneath volcanic ash from an eruption of the Shala volcano dated to about 233,000 years ago, making it at least that old. At Herto in the Middle Awash, skulls about 160,000 years old, described in 2003 as Homo sapiens idaltu, show early modern humans with some archaic traits and cut marks suggesting mortuary handling of the dead. Together with Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, these finds document the long, Africa-wide emergence of anatomically modern humans.

title: Early forays out of Africa: Apidima and Misliya
summary: Fossils from Greece and Israel hint that Homo sapiens left Africa in early waves long before the main dispersal, though these groups left few descendants.
description: A partial skull from Apidima Cave in southern Greece, dated in 2019 to about 210,000 years ago, was identified as an early Homo sapiens, while an upper jaw from Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel, Israel, dates to about 194,000–177,000 years ago. Burials at Skhul and Qafzeh in the Levant show that modern humans lived there between roughly 120,000 and 90,000 years ago. These finds suggest repeated early excursions out of Africa, perhaps during humid phases that greened the Sinai and Arabia. Genetic evidence, however, indicates that nearly all living non-Africans descend from a much later dispersal, so most of these early populations appear to have died out or been absorbed.
mainstreamView: The Misliya, Skhul and Qafzeh fossils are widely accepted as early Homo sapiens outside Africa. The identification of Apidima 1 is contested because the skull is fragmentary and distorted, and some researchers doubt that it is a modern human. Most specialists agree that these early groups contributed little or nothing to the ancestry of present-day populations.

title: Homo floresiensis, the 'hobbits' of Flores
summary: On the Indonesian island of Flores, a diminutive human species about a metre tall made stone tools until roughly 50,000 years ago.
description: Homo floresiensis was described in 2004 from the skeleton LB1 and other remains found in Liang Bua cave on Flores, Indonesia. Adults stood about 1.1 m tall and had brains roughly a third the size of ours, yet made stone tools. Initial dates as young as 18,000 years were revised in 2016: the skeletal remains are about 100,000–60,000 years old and the species' tools disappear about 50,000 years ago, close to when modern humans reached the region. Fossils from Mata Menge show that small hominins lived on Flores 700,000 years ago, and whether the species descends from a dwarfed Homo erectus or an earlier hominin is still debated.

title: Denisovans and a hybrid child at Denisova Cave
summary: A bone fragment from Siberia's Denisova Cave belonged to a girl whose mother was a Neanderthal and whose father was a Denisovan.
description: Denisovans, an archaic human group known mainly from DNA, were identified in 2010 from a finger bone in Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of Siberia; fossils since attributed to them include a jawbone from Baishiya Karst Cave on the Tibetan Plateau and the Harbin skull from northeastern China. Genome sequencing in 2018 revealed that a roughly 90,000-year-old bone fragment, Denisova 11 or 'Denny', came from a first-generation hybrid with a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Denisovans also interbred with modern humans: people in New Guinea and Australia carry several per cent Denisovan DNA, and a Denisovan variant of the EPAS1 gene helps Tibetans live at high altitude. Their full range, appearance and relationship to other Asian fossils remain active research questions.

title: Engraved ochre at Blombos Cave
summary: Pieces of red ochre engraved with crosshatched lines in a South African cave are among the oldest known abstract designs made by Homo sapiens.
description: Blombos Cave, on the southern Cape coast of South Africa, has yielded pieces of red ochre deliberately engraved with crosshatched patterns, dated to about 77,000 years ago, together with beads of perforated Nassarius shells about 75,000 years old. Older layers contain a toolkit for making an ochre-rich paint, mixed and stored in abalone shells about 100,000 years ago, and a later silcrete flake bears a crosshatched drawing in ochre crayon dated to about 73,000 years ago. These finds, together with evidence from sites such as Pinnacle Point and Diepkloof, helped overturn the idea that symbolic behaviour appeared suddenly in Europe about 40,000 years ago, showing instead that it developed gradually in Africa.

title: Toba supereruption
summary: The eruption of Toba in Sumatra, one of the largest known volcanic eruptions, blanketed South Asia in ash and left a caldera about 100 km long.
description: Around 74,000 years ago the Youngest Toba Tuff eruption on Sumatra ejected an estimated 2,800 cubic kilometres or more of magma, forming the caldera now filled by Lake Toba and spreading ash across India, the Arabian Sea and the South China Sea. In the 1990s researchers proposed that a resulting 'volcanic winter' reduced the human population to a few thousand breeding individuals, a genetic bottleneck. That catastrophe hypothesis is now widely doubted: stone-tool making continued above and below the ash at Jwalapuram in India, people at Pinnacle Point in South Africa persisted through the event, and Lake Malawi sediments show no severe cooling in East Africa. The eruption's size is undisputed, but its effects on climate and on human evolution remain debated.

title: Out of Africa: the main human dispersal
summary: A population of Homo sapiens left Africa and spread across Eurasia; virtually all living people outside Africa descend from it.
description: Genetic studies of living and ancient people show that almost all present-day populations outside Africa descend from a group that left the continent roughly 70,000 to 50,000 years ago, probably crossing into Arabia via the Sinai or the Bab-el-Mandeb strait. These migrants interbred with Neanderthals soon after leaving, and within a few tens of millennia their descendants had reached southern Asia, Australia, Europe and northeast Asia. Earlier forays from Africa left traces in the fossil record but contributed little to living populations. The exact timing, the route or routes taken and the role of climate in opening the way remain debated, with some researchers favouring a single dispersal and others several pulses.
wikipedia: Recent African origin of modern humans

title: First people reach Australia
summary: Seafaring Homo sapiens crossed open water to reach Sahul, the combined Australia–New Guinea landmass, by at least 50,000 years ago.
description: Even at times of low sea level, reaching Sahul from Southeast Asia required several open-water crossings, making it one of the earliest clear examples of deliberate seafaring. Luminescence dates from the Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land suggest people were present about 65,000 years ago, while many sites across the continent show occupation by 50,000–45,000 years ago. At Lake Mungo in New South Wales, the burials known as Mungo Lady and Mungo Man, about 40,000 years old, include one of the oldest known cremations and an ochre-covered body. Aboriginal Australian cultures descend from these first arrivals and represent one of the longest continuous cultural traditions on Earth.
mainstreamView: Human presence in Australia by about 50,000–47,000 years ago is widely accepted. The 65,000-year date from Madjedbebe is contested: critics argue that artefacts may have moved down through the sandy sediments and that the date is older than most genetic estimates for the out-of-Africa dispersal, while the excavators defend their stratigraphy and dating.

title: Oldest figurative cave paintings in Sulawesi
summary: A painting of three human-like figures and a wild pig in Leang Karampuang cave, Indonesia, is at least 51,200 years old, the oldest known figurative art.
description: Limestone caves in the Maros-Pangkep karst of southern Sulawesi contain hundreds of hand stencils and paintings of animals. Uranium-series dating of mineral crusts that formed over the pigment gives minimum ages: a warty pig at Leang Tedongnge is at least 45,500 years old, and a scene at Leang Karampuang showing human-like figures interacting with a pig, published in 2024, is at least 51,200 years old. These dates make Sulawesi's art older than any known figurative painting in Europe. They suggest that narrative imagery was already part of the culture of the first modern humans to spread through island Southeast Asia.

title: Modern humans interbreed with Neanderthals
summary: Shortly after leaving Africa, Homo sapiens interbred with Neanderthals; roughly 1–2% of the DNA of living non-Africans is Neanderthal in origin.
description: The first Neanderthal genome, published in 2010, showed that people outside Africa carry a small fraction of Neanderthal DNA, inherited from interbreeding soon after modern humans left Africa, probably in western Asia. Analyses of ancient genomes published in 2024 place the main episode at roughly 50,000–43,500 years ago. Early modern humans such as a 45,000-year-old man from Ust'-Ishim in Siberia and individuals from Ranis in Germany carried longer Neanderthal segments, and the Oase 1 jaw from Romania belonged to someone with a Neanderthal ancestor only four to six generations back. Some inherited variants still affect immunity, skin and disease risk today, and gene flow in the other direction, into Neanderthals, is also documented.
wikipedia: Interbreeding between archaic and modern humans

title: Venus of Hohle Fels and the first figurines
summary: Mammoth-ivory carvings from Germany's Swabian Jura, including the Venus of Hohle Fels and the Lion-man, are among the oldest known figurative sculptures.
description: Caves in the Swabian Jura of southwestern Germany preserve some of the earliest art made by modern humans in Europe. The Venus of Hohle Fels, a 6-cm mammoth-ivory figure of a woman with exaggerated breasts and hips found in 2008, dates to about 40,000 years ago and is the oldest undisputed sculpture of a human figure. Nearby caves yielded the Lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel, part human and part lion, and flutes of bird bone and ivory about 40,000 years old. Female 'Venus' figurines later became widespread from France to Siberia during the Gravettian, about 33,000–21,000 years ago, including the Venus of Willendorf from Austria and the ceramic Venus of Dolní Věstonice from Moravia. Their meaning, whether as fertility symbols, self-portraits or something else, remains uncertain.

title: Neanderthals disappear
summary: Neanderthals, who had lived across Europe and western Asia for over 300,000 years, vanished about 40,000 years ago as modern humans spread.
description: Radiocarbon dating of sites from Spain to Russia, published in 2014, indicates that Neanderthals disappeared between about 41,000 and 39,000 years ago, after overlapping with incoming modern humans in parts of Europe for several thousand years. Later dates of 28,000–24,000 years from Gorham's Cave in Gibraltar and other Iberian sites have been proposed but are disputed. The causes are debated and probably combined: competition with Homo sapiens, small and fragmented populations, climate instability during the last glacial period and absorption through interbreeding. Neanderthals, who buried some of their dead and used pigments and ornaments, live on genetically in most living people.

title: Paintings of Chauvet Cave
summary: Lions, rhinoceroses, horses and mammoths painted in France's Chauvet Cave some 36,000 years ago are among the most accomplished early artworks known.
description: Discovered in the Ardèche gorge of southern France in 1994, the Chauvet-Pont d'Arc Cave contains hundreds of painted and engraved animals, many of them dangerous species such as cave lions, cave bears and woolly rhinoceroses that are rare in later cave art. Radiocarbon dating of charcoal and other traces indicates two phases of human activity, about 37,000–33,500 and 31,000–28,000 years ago, with most of the art belonging to the first. Its use of shading, perspective and scraped surfaces showed that sophisticated painting existed early in the Upper Palaeolithic of Europe. A rockfall sealed the entrance, preserving the cave's contents, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.

title: Last Glacial Maximum
summary: Ice sheets reached their greatest extent of the last ice age, lowering sea level by about 120 m and exposing land bridges between continents.
description: During the Last Glacial Maximum, the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets covered most of Canada and the northern United States, and the Fennoscandian and British–Irish ice sheets covered northern Europe. Global average temperature was roughly 6 °C lower than before industrialisation, and sea level stood about 120–130 m below today's, joining Siberia to Alaska as Beringia, Britain to Europe, and New Guinea to Australia as Sahul. Large areas became cold steppe and desert, and human populations in Europe retreated to southern refugia such as Iberia and the Balkans. Deglaciation began about 19,000 years ago as rising Northern Hemisphere summer sunshine and increasing carbon dioxide began melting the ice.

title: Ice Age footprints at White Sands
summary: Human footprints in an ancient lakebed in New Mexico, dated to 23,000–21,000 years ago, suggest people were in North America during the last ice age.
description: Dozens of human footprints, many made by teenagers and children, were left in soft sediments on the shore of ancient Lake Otero, now in White Sands National Park, alongside tracks of mammoths and giant ground sloths. Radiocarbon dating of seeds of the aquatic plant Ruppia cirrhosa from layers above and below the prints, published in 2021, gave ages of about 23,000–21,000 years. Follow-up studies in 2023 obtained similar ages from conifer pollen and from luminescence dating of quartz grains. If correct, the footprints show that people reached North America before the ice sheets closed the inland routes, thousands of years earlier than most previously accepted sites.
mainstreamView: Many archaeologists now accept the dates, but some argue that the aquatic seeds could carry an 'old carbon' reservoir effect and that the pollen and luminescence results do not fully settle the question. Because no stone tools or campsites accompany the prints, and few other sites support such an early arrival, a human presence in the Americas before about 16,000 years ago remains contested.

title: World's oldest pottery at Xianrendong
summary: Fragments of fired clay vessels from Xianrendong Cave in southern China, about 20,000 years old, are the earliest known pottery.
description: Radiocarbon dating published in 2012 showed that potsherds from Xianrendong Cave in Jiangxi Province were made about 20,000–19,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum and some 10,000 years before farming began in the region. The pots were probably used by mobile hunter-gatherers for cooking, perhaps to extract fat and nutrients from bone or to prepare shellfish and plants in a cold climate. Pottery of similar antiquity appears at Yuchanyan in Hunan, about 18,000 years ago, and among the earliest Jōmon of Japan, about 16,000 years ago. The finds show that pottery was invented by East Asian foragers long before it became part of the Neolithic farming package in western Asia.

title: Solutrean hypothesis: Ice Age Europeans in America
summary: A minority hypothesis holds that Solutrean people from Ice Age France and Spain crossed the North Atlantic along the sea ice and founded the Clovis culture.
description: Developed by archaeologists Dennis Stanford and Bruce Bradley, notably in their 2012 book 'Across Atlantic Ice', the hypothesis proposes that hunters of the Solutrean culture of southwestern Europe, about 22,000–17,000 years ago, travelled along the edge of the North Atlantic sea ice hunting seals and reached eastern North America. Proponents point to resemblances between Solutrean and Clovis bifacial flint points, including a shared overshot flaking technique, and to a few contested artefacts from the eastern seaboard such as a stone blade dredged from the seabed off Virginia. The idea has attracted wide public attention but very little support among archaeologists and geneticists.
mainstreamView: Ancient genomes, including that of the Clovis-associated Anzick child from Montana, show that Native Americans descend from East Asian and Siberian populations, with no detectable ancestry from Ice Age western Europe. The Solutrean and Clovis cultures are separated by roughly 5,000 years and an ocean, and their technological resemblances are explained as convergence. The age and origin of the eastern 'Solutrean-like' finds are also disputed.

title: Lascaux cave paintings
summary: Nearly 6,000 figures of horses, aurochs, deer and abstract signs were painted and engraved in Lascaux cave in southwestern France around 17,000 years ago.
description: Found by four teenagers in 1940 near Montignac in the Dordogne, Lascaux is the most famous example of Upper Palaeolithic cave art, with its Hall of the Bulls dominated by aurochs more than 5 m long. The art is attributed to the early Magdalenian culture and is usually dated to around 17,000 years ago, though some researchers argue for a somewhat earlier origin. Artists used mineral pigments, scaffolding and lamps burning animal fat to decorate the walls and ceilings. Opened to the public in 1948, the cave was closed in 1963 after visitors' breath and lighting encouraged the growth of algae and fungi, and visitors now see detailed replicas.

title: People spread into the Americas
summary: Descendants of Siberian and East Asian populations moved from Beringia into the Americas and reached southern Chile by about 14,500 years ago.
description: Genetic evidence indicates that the ancestors of Native Americans diverged from East Asian and Siberian populations and spent some time in Beringia, the now-drowned land bridge between Siberia and Alaska, before moving south, most likely along the Pacific coast as the ice retreated and later through an ice-free corridor east of the Rocky Mountains. Sites such as Cooper's Ferry in Idaho, the Paisley Caves in Oregon, Page-Ladson in Florida and Monte Verde in Chile show people were present by about 16,000–14,500 years ago, before the Clovis culture. The once-dominant 'Clovis first' model, which put the first Americans at about 13,000 years ago, has been abandoned. Whether people arrived much earlier, as claimed for the footprints at White Sands in New Mexico, is still debated.

title: Natufian culture: early forager villages
summary: Foragers in the Levant built some of the world's first permanent villages, harvested wild cereals and baked bread thousands of years before farming.
description: The Natufian culture, named after Wadi en-Natuf in the West Bank, flourished across the Levant from about 15,000 to 11,500 years ago. Natufians lived in settlements of round, semi-subterranean stone houses such as 'Ain Mallaha (Eynan) in the Jordan Valley, harvested wild wheat, barley and legumes with sickles, and buried their dead beneath and around their homes, in one case a woman with a puppy. Charred crumbs of flatbread about 14,400 years old from Shubayqa 1 in Jordan predate farming by at least 4,000 years. Natufian sedentism set the stage for the domestication of plants and animals in the following Pre-Pottery Neolithic.

title: Monte Verde: pre-Clovis settlement in Chile
summary: A waterlogged camp in southern Chile, occupied about 14,500 years ago, proved that people reached South America before the Clovis culture.
description: Excavated by Tom Dillehay from the late 1970s, the Monte Verde II site near Puerto Montt preserved wooden foundations of a long tent-like dwelling, hearths, stone tools, mastodon meat and remains of seaweeds and medicinal plants beneath a peat bog. Its age of about 14,500 years, more than a millennium older than the Clovis sites of North America, was accepted by a panel of leading archaeologists, including former sceptics, who visited in 1997, a turning point in abandoning the 'Clovis first' model. Seaweeds brought from the coast support the idea of an early migration along the Pacific coast. Claims for a much older occupation layer, Monte Verde I, about 33,000 years old, are not widely accepted.

title: Dogs: the first domesticated animal
dateLabel: Oberkassel dog c. 14,200 years ago (domestication earlier)
summary: A dog buried with two people at Bonn-Oberkassel, Germany, about 14,200 years ago is the oldest undisputed domestic dog; domestication probably began earlier.
description: Dogs descend from a population of grey wolves and were domesticated by hunter-gatherers well before farming, making them the first domestic animal. The oldest generally accepted dog comes from a grave at Bonn-Oberkassel, Germany, where a young dog that had evidently been nursed through canine distemper was buried with a man and a woman about 14,200 years ago. Genetic studies suggest that domestication began somewhere in Eurasia more than 15,000 years ago, perhaps among people in Siberia around 23,000 years ago. By the end of the Ice Age dogs accompanied people across Eurasia and into the Americas.
mainstreamView: Researchers agree that dogs were domesticated from wolves by hunter-gatherers before the advent of farming, but proposed dates range from about 15,000 to more than 30,000 years ago. Claimed 'Palaeolithic dogs' from sites such as Goyet in Belgium, about 36,000 years old, are disputed and may be unusual wolves, and genetic studies disagree on whether domestication happened in Siberia, East Asia, Europe or in more than one place.

title: Jebel Sahaba: early evidence of warfare
summary: A Nile valley cemetery in Sudan holding men, women and children with embedded stone projectiles is among the oldest evidence of repeated violent conflict.
description: Excavated in the 1960s ahead of the flooding of Lake Nubia behind the Aswan High Dam, the Jebel Sahaba cemetery contained the remains of 61 individuals. A re-analysis published in 2021 found healed and unhealed injuries, many from arrows or spears, on about two-thirds of the skeletons, suggesting repeated episodes of violence rather than a single battle. Redating places the burials at least 13,400 years ago, during a time of environmental stress along the Nile at the end of the last ice age. At Nataruk in Kenya, about 10,000 years ago, a group of foragers was killed in what some researchers interpret as an inter-group massacre.

title: Megafauna vanish from the Americas
summary: Mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, sabre-toothed cats and native horses died out as the ice age ended and people spread across the Americas.
description: Around the end of the last ice age, North and South America lost more than 70% of their genera of large mammals, including mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, glyptodonts, Smilodon, dire wolves, horses and camels. The losses coincided with rapid climate swings at the end of the Pleistocene and with the spread of human hunters, including the Clovis culture, whose distinctive fluted points are found with mammoth and mastodon remains. Similar extinction waves struck Australia around 45,000 years ago and northern Eurasia between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, while Africa lost comparatively few species. Fossil deposits such as the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles preserve many of the vanished animals.
mainstreamView: Most researchers accept that both climate change and human hunting played roles, but they disagree on the balance. The close timing of extinctions with human arrival on several continents favours a strong human role, whereas others emphasise habitat change during deglaciation; a cosmic impact has also been proposed but is not widely accepted.

title: Younger Dryas cold snap
summary: A sudden return to near-glacial cold in the Northern Hemisphere interrupted the warming at the end of the last ice age for about 1,200 years.
description: Named after the Arctic flower Dryas octopetala, whose pollen reappears in European lake sediments of the time, the Younger Dryas brought temperatures in Greenland and around the North Atlantic back towards ice-age levels within decades. The leading explanation is a weakening of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, probably triggered by meltwater from the North American ice sheets flowing into the North Atlantic or Arctic Ocean. Its effects reached far beyond the North Atlantic, including drier conditions in the Levant during the late Natufian period, shortly before the first farming. The cold interval ended abruptly about 11,700 years ago, marking the start of the Holocene.

title: Younger Dryas impact hypothesis
summary: Some scientists propose that fragments of a comet exploded over North America about 12,800 years ago, triggering the Younger Dryas and megafaunal extinctions.
description: First proposed in 2007 by Richard Firestone and colleagues, the hypothesis attributes the Younger Dryas cooling, the end of the Clovis culture and the extinction of American megafauna to airbursts or impacts of a fragmenting comet. Supporters cite a thin sediment layer at the onset of the Younger Dryas, at sites such as Murray Springs in Arizona and Abu Hureyra in Syria, reported to contain platinum spikes, magnetic microspherules, nanodiamonds and melt-glass. A group of researchers continues to publish in support of the idea, while many others have challenged it, making it one of the most contested ideas in Quaternary science.
mainstreamView: Most Quaternary scientists and archaeologists reject the hypothesis. Independent teams have often failed to reproduce the proposed markers or have found them at other levels, no crater of the right age has been identified, the dark 'black mat' layers are explained by local wetland conditions, and megafaunal extinctions and Clovis changes were not synchronous. The Younger Dryas itself is well explained by changes in Atlantic Ocean circulation, and similar cold events occurred during earlier deglaciations without impacts.

title: Claimed lost Ice Age civilisation
summary: Popular authors claim an advanced Ice Age civilisation was wiped out by a cosmic cataclysm 12,800 years ago, its survivors teaching early farmers.
description: Writers such as Graham Hancock, in books including 'Fingerprints of the Gods' (1995) and 'Magicians of the Gods' (2015) and the 2022 Netflix series 'Ancient Apocalypse', argue that a technologically advanced, seafaring civilisation existed during the last ice age. In this account it was destroyed by comet impacts and floods at the onset of the Younger Dryas about 12,800 years ago, and survivors passed on astronomy, monument building and agriculture to hunter-gatherers, as supposedly shown at Göbekli Tepe in Turkey and Gunung Padang in Indonesia. Proponents also cite flood myths from many cultures and alleged astronomical alignments of later monuments. The idea is popular on television and podcasts but is rejected by archaeologists.
mainstreamView: No artefacts, settlements, metals, crops, domesticated animals or pollution traces of an advanced Ice Age society have been found anywhere, although the period is documented by thousands of excavated sites. Göbekli Tepe was built by local hunter-gatherers whose tools, food remains and houses have been excavated on site, and a 2023 paper claiming Gunung Padang was a 27,000-year-old pyramid was retracted in 2024 because its dates came from soil with no evidence of human activity. Farming emerged gradually over thousands of years in several regions, and flood myths are better explained by local floods and shared storytelling.

title: Orion correlation theory: Giza and the sky of 10,500 BCE
summary: Authors Robert Bauval and Graham Hancock claim the Giza pyramids and Sphinx mirror Orion's Belt and Leo as the sky looked around 10,500 BCE.
description: In 1989 the author Robert Bauval proposed that the three main pyramids at Giza, with the smaller pyramid of Menkaure slightly offset, reproduce the pattern of the three stars of Orion's Belt, a constellation the ancient Egyptians associated with the god Osiris. In 'The Orion Mystery' (1994, with Adrian Gilbert) and 'Keeper of Genesis' (1996, with Graham Hancock) the idea was extended: the Nile was said to stand for the Milky Way and the lion-bodied Sphinx for the constellation Leo, and the whole arrangement was claimed to match the sky at dawn on the spring equinox around 10,500 BCE. Bauval and Hancock argued that the Giza plan was therefore conceived or begun in that era and linked it to a lost Ice Age civilisation. The theory reached a wide audience through books and television documentaries and is often combined with the claim that weathering on the Sphinx proves it far older than the Old Kingdom.
mainstreamView: Egyptologists date the pyramids to the Fourth Dynasty, about 2600–2500 BCE: they were built as separate tomb complexes by Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure within less than a century and sited according to the terrain and nearby quarries, and no building activity of around 10,500 BCE has been found at Giza. The astronomers Ed Krupp and Anthony Fairall found that the match with Orion's Belt is loose, since the angle of the belt differs from that of the pyramids and the layout fits only if the map of Giza is turned upside down. They also pointed out that the spring-equinox sun around 10,500 BCE rose in Virgo rather than Leo, and that the zodiac constellations were unknown in Egypt until the Graeco-Roman period.

title: Holocene begins
summary: The abrupt end of the Younger Dryas opened the Holocene, the warm, stable interglacial in which farming and all later civilisations arose.
description: The base of the Holocene Epoch is formally defined by a marker in the NorthGRIP ice core from central Greenland, dated to 11,700 years before 2000 CE, where chemical and isotopic signals record rapid warming within a few decades. Ice sheets in North America and Scandinavia continued to retreat for thousands of years, and global sea level rose by tens of metres until about 7,000 years ago, drowning coastal plains. The comparatively warm and stable climate that followed is thought to have made the adoption of agriculture possible, independently, in several regions. The Holocene is the current epoch; a proposal to define a separate Anthropocene epoch was rejected in 2024.

title: Atlantis sinks, according to Plato
summary: Plato described a powerful island empire beyond the Pillars of Heracles that sank into the sea in a single day and night, 9,000 years before Solon.
description: Atlantis appears in Plato's dialogues Timaeus and Critias, written around 360 BCE, in which the Athenian statesman Solon is said to have learned from Egyptian priests of a great naval power that attacked Athens 9,000 years earlier and was then swallowed by the sea. Since the 19th century, especially after Ignatius Donnelly's 'Atlantis: The Antediluvian World' (1882), writers have placed a real Atlantis in the Atlantic, the Caribbean, Antarctica and many other locations, often presenting it as the source of all later civilisations. Others identify it with the Bronze Age Minoan civilisation, struck by the eruption of Thera around 1600 BCE. Plato's date falls near the end of the last ice age, which is why Atlantis is often linked to claims of a lost Ice Age civilisation.
mainstreamView: Classical scholars almost universally regard Atlantis as a fictional device Plato invented to illustrate his ideas about the ideal state, not a historical report, and no earlier source mentions it. Archaeology shows that around 9600 BCE people everywhere lived as hunter-gatherers or very early cultivators and Athens did not exist, while seafloor mapping has found no sunken continent in the Atlantic, whose floor is young oceanic crust formed by seafloor spreading.

title: Göbekli Tepe's monumental enclosures
summary: Hunter-gatherers in southeastern Turkey raised circles of carved T-shaped limestone pillars up to 5.5 m tall, among the oldest known monumental buildings.
description: Excavated from 1995 by Klaus Schmidt of the German Archaeological Institute, Göbekli Tepe sits on a limestone ridge near Şanlıurfa and dates from the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, about 9500–8000 BCE. Its large round enclosures are ringed by T-shaped pillars, some weighing about 10 tonnes, carved with foxes, boars, snakes, vultures and stylised human arms and hands, suggesting the pillars represent human or ancestral figures. Schmidt interpreted the site as a ceremonial centre built before farming, but more recent excavations have found houses, cisterns and evidence of daily life, showing that it was also a settlement. Göbekli Tepe and related sites nearby, such as Karahan Tepe, show that monumental architecture and complex symbolism arose among foragers on the threshold of agriculture.

title: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent
summary: People in the Fertile Crescent began cultivating and domesticating wheat, barley, lentils and peas, starting the transition from foraging to farming.
description: Soon after the end of the Younger Dryas, communities in the arc of land from the southern Levant through southeastern Turkey to the Zagros Mountains began cultivating wild cereals and legumes. Over the following two to three millennia, eight 'founder crops' (emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax) became genetically domesticated, with seed heads that no longer shattered and depended on people for sowing. DNA studies trace einkorn wheat to the Karacadağ hills of southeastern Turkey, though domestication was a protracted process spread across several areas. Farming supported larger, permanent populations and spread from here into Europe, North Africa and South Asia, reaching Mehrgarh in Pakistan by about 7000 BCE. Agriculture was also invented independently in China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica, the Andes, eastern North America and sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Green Sahara: the African Humid Period
summary: Stronger monsoon rains turned much of the Sahara into grassland dotted with lakes, home to hunters, fishers and, later, cattle herders.
description: Changes in Earth's orbit increased Northern Hemisphere summer sunshine in the early Holocene, strengthening the West African monsoon and pushing rainfall far into the Sahara. Vegetation feedbacks amplified the change: savanna, wetlands and large lakes such as Lake Mega-Chad covered regions that are now desert, supporting hippos, crocodiles and elephants. People moved in, making some of Africa's earliest pottery at Ounjougou in Mali by about 9400 BCE and later herding cattle, sheep and goats, as recorded at sites such as Nabta Playa in Egypt and in the rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria. As the orbital forcing weakened, the region dried out between about 6,000 and 4,500 years ago, abruptly in some places and gradually in others, pushing herders towards the Nile valley and the Sahel shortly before the rise of Egyptian civilisation.

title: Rice and millet farming begin in China
summary: Villagers along the Yangtze began cultivating rice, and those on the Yellow River broomcorn and foxtail millet, founding East Asian agriculture.
description: China was one of the world's independent centres of plant domestication. In the lower Yangtze valley, sites of the Shangshan culture in Zhejiang show rice being gathered and cultivated from about 9000 BCE, and the grains gradually acquired the non-shattering domestic form over several thousand years, a process largely complete by about 5000–4000 BCE at sites such as Tianluoshan and Hemudu. In the drier north, storage pits at Cishan in Hebei contain broomcorn millet from about 8000 BCE, and millet farming underpinned the later Peiligang and Yangshao cultures of the Yellow River valley. At Jiahu in Henan, people around 7000 BCE brewed a fermented drink of rice, honey and fruit, among the oldest chemical evidence for an alcoholic beverage. Rice farming later spread through Southeast and South Asia and became a staple for a large share of humanity.

title: Goats, sheep, cattle and pigs domesticated
summary: Farmers in the Fertile Crescent domesticated goats, sheep, cattle and pigs from wild bezoar ibex, mouflon, aurochs and boar.
description: Changes in the age and sex of slaughtered animals and reductions in body size show that people in the northern Fertile Crescent began managing and domesticating animals around 9000–8000 BCE. Goats were domesticated from the bezoar ibex, notably in the Zagros Mountains at sites such as Ganj Dareh, and sheep from the Asiatic mouflon in southeastern Anatolia. Cattle were derived from aurochs in the upper Euphrates and Tigris valleys, according to one genetic study from as few as 80 animals, and pigs from wild boar at sites such as Çayönü. Humped zebu cattle were domesticated separately from Indian aurochs in South Asia, probably around Mehrgarh in Pakistan by about 7000–6000 BCE. Livestock provided meat and later milk, wool and traction, and spread with farmers into Europe and Africa.

title: Jericho's wall and tower
summary: At Tell es-Sultan near Jericho, Neolithic villagers built a massive stone wall and an 8.5-m stone tower, among the oldest monumental structures.
description: Jericho, at the spring-fed oasis of Tell es-Sultan in the Jordan Valley, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited places on Earth. In the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A period, a settlement of round mud-brick houses grew there, home to perhaps several hundred people who cultivated early domesticated cereals. Around 8000 BCE its inhabitants built a stone wall and a solid stone tower about 8.5 m high with an internal staircase of 22 steps, excavated by Kathleen Kenyon in the 1950s. Kenyon saw them as defences, but many archaeologists now think the wall protected against floods and the tower had ritual or communal purposes. Later Neolithic layers produced plastered human skulls with shell eyes, an early form of ancestor veneration.

title: Potatoes and llamas: farming begins in the Andes
summary: Andean peoples independently domesticated the potato in the highlands of southern Peru and Bolivia and later herded llamas and alpacas.
description: South America was one of the world's independent centres of domestication. Genetic studies trace the cultivated potato to wild species of the highlands of southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca, where it was probably domesticated between about 8000 and 5000 BCE, although tubers preserve poorly and the oldest securely identified remains, from Ancón on the Peruvian coast, date only to about 2500 BCE. In the Ñanchoc Valley of northern Peru people were already growing squash about 10,000 years ago and peanuts about 8,500 years ago, crops probably first domesticated elsewhere in South America. On the high puna grasslands, hunters of wild camelids gradually became herders, turning vicuñas into alpacas and guanacos into llamas, probably from about 6,000–7,000 years ago, and guinea pigs were domesticated for meat by about 5000 BCE. Quinoa, also domesticated around Lake Titicaca, potatoes and camelids later sustained Andean societies from Caral to Tiwanaku and the Inca.

title: Çatalhöyük, a Neolithic town in Anatolia
summary: Thousands of farmers lived in tightly packed mud-brick houses entered through their roofs at Çatalhöyük, one of the largest Neolithic settlements known.
description: Çatalhöyük, on the Konya Plain of south-central Turkey, was occupied for more than a millennium and at its height may have housed several thousand people. Its houses were built wall-to-wall with no streets, and residents moved across the rooftops and entered by ladders; interiors were decorated with wall paintings, plastered bull horns and reliefs, and the dead were buried beneath the floors. Excavations by James Mellaart in the 1960s and by Ian Hodder from 1993 found little evidence of public buildings or marked social hierarchy, suggesting a relatively egalitarian society. A wall painting interpreted as a town plan beneath an erupting volcano, possibly Hasan Dağ, may be one of the oldest known landscape images, though this reading is disputed. Çatalhöyük became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.

title: Maize domesticated from teosinte in Mexico
summary: Farmers in the Balsas River valley of southwestern Mexico began turning teosinte, a wild grass, into maize, later the staple crop of the Americas.
description: Genetic studies show that maize descends from Balsas teosinte, a wild grass whose few hard-cased kernels look little like a modern cob, and that it was domesticated once, in the central Balsas River valley about 9,000 years ago. Starch grains and phytoliths on stone tools from the Xihuatoxtla rock shelter in Guerrero confirm maize use there by about 8,700 years ago, and the oldest preserved cobs, from Guilá Naquitz Cave in Oaxaca, are about 6,250 years old. Squash had been domesticated in Mexico even earlier, about 10,000 years ago, and maize, beans and squash later became the core of the Mesoamerican milpa field system, the combination later known in North America as the 'Three Sisters'. Over millennia of selection, maize spread north and south through the Americas and became the foundation of civilisations such as the Olmec, Maya and Aztec.

title: Mehrgarh: early farming village in South Asia
dateLabel: c. 7000 BCE (some new dates suggest c. 5250 BCE)
summary: Villagers at Mehrgarh, below the Bolan Pass in Pakistan, grew barley and wheat and herded goats, sheep and cattle, among South Asia's earliest farmers.
description: Discovered in 1974 by a French team led by Jean-François and Catherine Jarrige, Mehrgarh lies on the Kachi plain of Balochistan, on a route between the Iranian plateau and the Indus valley. Its earliest village, built before pottery came into use, had mud-brick houses and granaries and yielded six-row barley, einkorn and emmer wheat and the bones of goats, sheep and cattle, while burials with ornaments of turquoise, seashell and lapis lazuli from Badakhshan in Afghanistan show long-distance exchange. Molars with neatly drilled holes from its Neolithic cemetery, reported in 2006, are among the earliest evidence of dentistry. The excavators dated the first village to before 7000 BCE, but more recent radiocarbon dates on human teeth place it around 5250–4650 BCE, so its age is now debated. Wheat, sheep and goats probably came from the Near East, whereas zebu cattle and perhaps barley were domesticated locally, and the site's later phases lead towards the Indus Valley Civilisation.

title: Ubaid period: irrigation farmers and Eridu's temples
summary: Farmers settled the alluvial plain of southern Mesopotamia, irrigated their fields and built mud-brick temples at Eridu, laying foundations for Sumer.
description: The Ubaid period is named after Tell al-'Ubaid near Ur, excavated by Henry Hall and Leonard Woolley from 1919, and is recognised by buff pottery painted with dark geometric designs. Its oldest known site, Tell el-'Oueili, dates to about 6500 BCE, and Ubaid villages are the earliest known settlements on the southern Mesopotamian plain, where low rainfall made farming depend on water drawn from the Euphrates and Tigris. Eridu, founded around 5400 BCE on a sand dune near the then coast of the Persian Gulf and remembered in Sumerian tradition as the first city, preserves a sequence of 18 superimposed mud-brick shrines and temples, growing from a small chapel into large tripartite buildings beneath the later temple of the god Enki. Ubaid pottery and customs spread north into Syria and southeastern Anatolia and south along the Gulf coast, where the site of H3 in Kuwait has yielded the earliest known image of a sailing boat. Larger settlements, temple institutions and growing social inequality during the Ubaid set the stage for the cities of the following Uruk period.

title: Anatolian farmers bring farming to Europe
summary: Descendants of Neolithic Anatolian farmers spread through the Balkans and along the Danube and Mediterranean, bringing crops and livestock to Europe.
description: Farming reached Europe from western Anatolia, and villages with cereal fields, sheep and goats appeared in Greece and the southern Balkans by about 6500 BCE. Ancient DNA shows that this was largely a migration of people rather than only the spread of an idea: Europe's early farmers descended mainly from Neolithic Anatolian populations and mixed only gradually with the hunter-gatherers already living there. One stream followed the Danube into central Europe, where the Linear Pottery culture (LBK), with its timber longhouses up to about 45 m long, spread from Hungary to the Paris Basin and Ukraine from about 5500 BCE, while another moved along the Mediterranean coasts with Impressed and Cardial Ware pottery to Italy, southern France and Iberia. Farming reached Britain, Ireland and southern Scandinavia only around 4000 BCE, after a long pause at the frontier with Mesolithic foragers. Mass graves such as the Talheim death pit in Germany, about 5000 BCE, show that the expansion was not always peaceful.

title: Rising seas drown Doggerland
summary: The North Sea flooded Doggerland, the lowland that had joined Britain to continental Europe, possibly finished off by the Storegga Slide tsunami.
description: During the last ice age the southern North Sea was dry land, and as the ice sheets melted, rising seas gradually turned this region, now called Doggerland, into a low plain of rivers, marshes and lakes inhabited by Mesolithic hunter-gatherers. Fishing trawlers have dragged up mammoth bones, peat and artefacts from the seabed, including a barbed antler point recovered in 1931 between the Leman and Ower banks. As sea level kept rising, Doggerland shrank to a low archipelago and Britain became an island. Around 6200 BCE the Storegga Slide, a huge underwater landslide off Norway, sent a tsunami across the North Sea that probably struck what remained of Doggerland, though recent work suggests some islands survived for a while longer.

title: Indigenous Aryanism: the 'Out of India' claim
summary: Proponents claim Indo-European languages spread out of India rather than into it, and that Vedic Aryans built the Indus Valley Civilisation.
description: Indigenous Aryanism, also called the 'Out of India' theory, rejects the mainstream view that Indo-Aryan languages reached South Asia through migrations from Central Asia in the 2nd millennium BCE. Writers such as Koenraad Elst, who placed the Proto-Indo-Europeans in the Punjab in the 6th millennium BCE, and Shrikant Talageri argue that the Indo-European languages radiated outwards from India, that the Rigveda was composed in the 3rd millennium BCE or earlier, and that the Indus Valley Civilisation was Vedic. Proponents identify the mighty Sarasvati river of the Rigveda with the Ghaggar-Hakra, which had largely dried up by about 2000 BCE, and cite claimed early horse bones and the cart burials at Sinauli. The idea draws on traditional Puranic chronology, partly arose as a reaction to colonial-era 'Aryan invasion' narratives, and has become influential in Hindu nationalist politics.
mainstreamView: Mainstream linguists, archaeologists and geneticists reject the theory. Comparative linguistics places the Indo-European homeland on the Pontic–Caspian steppe and shows that Indo-Aryan shares a common Indo-Iranian ancestor with the languages of Iran, while the horses and spoked-wheel chariots central to the Rigveda fit the 2nd millennium BCE, not the Harappan cities, where horses are absent from the art and rare or doubtful among animal bones. Ancient DNA shows that steppe-related ancestry entered South Asia during the 2nd millennium BCE and is absent from the genome of a woman buried at the Harappan city of Rakhigarhi. Current models describe gradual migration and language shift rather than the discredited idea of a violent 'Aryan invasion'.

title: Black Sea deluge hypothesis
summary: Geologists proposed that rising Mediterranean waters burst through the Bosporus around 5600 BCE, rapidly flooding a freshwater lake to form today's Black Sea.
description: In 1997 marine geologists William Ryan and Walter Pitman proposed that during and after the last ice age the Black Sea was an isolated freshwater lake lying far below global sea level. In their scenario, rising Mediterranean waters overtopped the Bosporus sill around 5600 BCE and poured in with enormous force, raising the lake by tens of metres within a few years and drowning large areas of coastal land. Supporting evidence included submerged shorelines and an abrupt switch from freshwater to marine molluscs in seafloor sediments. They suggested the catastrophe could have dispersed early farming peoples and inspired flood stories such as those of Gilgamesh and Noah.
mainstreamView: A catastrophic flood remains contested. Some sediment and shoreline studies support a rapid reconnection, but others indicate that the Black Sea was not far below the Bosporus sill, that the connection began earlier, around 9,000–8,000 years ago, and that the change was gradual or happened in steps. There is no direct archaeological evidence linking it to population movements, and links to the Noah or Gilgamesh flood stories are speculative.

title: Chinchorro: the world's oldest artificial mummies
summary: Fishing communities of the Atacama coast in Chile and Peru began artificially mummifying their dead, the earliest known deliberate mummification.
description: The Chinchorro people were hunter-fisher-gatherers who lived along the Pacific coast of the Atacama Desert from about 7000 BCE. From about 5000 BCE they began removing the skin, organs and muscles of the dead, reinforcing the skeleton with sticks and reeds, and remodelling the body with clay, ash and plant fibre before covering it with skin and painting it black or red. Unlike in Egypt, the practice was applied to people of all ages and social ranks, including infants and fetuses. More than 280 mummies have been recovered, and the Chinchorro sites were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

title: Kuk Swamp: early farming in New Guinea
summary: In the highlands of New Guinea, people independently developed agriculture, draining wetlands and planting mounds of taro and bananas.
description: Kuk Swamp, in the Wahgi Valley near Mount Hagen in Papua New Guinea, preserves evidence for one of the world's independent origins of agriculture. Pits, stake-holes and channels suggest plant exploitation and possibly cultivation on the swamp margin about 10,000 years ago, and mounds for planting crops such as taro were built by about 7,000–6,400 years ago, when banana phytoliths become abundant. Ditched drainage systems followed after about 4,000 years ago. Bananas, sugarcane and some yams were first domesticated in the New Guinea region, and Kuk was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.

title: First copper smelting in the Balkans
summary: At Belovode in Serbia, Vinča culture metalworkers smelted copper from ore about 7,000 years ago, among the earliest securely dated smelting known.
description: People had hammered native copper into beads and awls since about 8000 BCE in Anatolia and the Near East, but extracting metal from ore by smelting was a major technological advance. Slag, malachite ore and copper droplets from Belovode, a Vinča culture settlement in eastern Serbia, were dated in 2010 to about 5000 BCE, with possibly similarly early smelting in Iran and Anatolia. The Copper Age that followed saw extensive copper mining at Rudna Glava in Serbia and Ai Bunar in Bulgaria, and the Varna Necropolis on Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, about 4500 BCE, holds the world's oldest large hoard of worked gold, revealing marked social inequality. Copper and later bronze working spread across Eurasia and transformed tools, weapons, trade and the display of status.

title: Carnac stones and the megaliths of Atlantic Europe
summary: Neolithic communities in Brittany erected more than 3,000 standing stones in long rows near Carnac, part of a megalithic tradition along Atlantic Europe.
description: The alignments of Ménec, Kermario and Kerlescan near Carnac in southern Brittany form the largest collection of standing stones in the world, accompanied by burial mounds, dolmens and giant menhirs such as the now-broken Grand Menhir of Er Grah. Megalith building in Brittany began around 4800–4500 BCE with chambered cairns such as Barnenez, among the earliest in Europe, and most of the Carnac rows probably date from about 4500–3300 BCE. A 2019 radiocarbon study argued that megalithic architecture originated in northwest France and spread by sea along the Atlantic coasts. The tradition later produced passage tombs such as Newgrange in Ireland, around 3200 BCE, and stone circles such as Stonehenge. The purpose of the stone rows, whether ritual, astronomical or territorial, remains unknown.

title: Proto-Indo-European speakers and their homeland
summary: The ancestor of languages from Hindi to English was probably spoken around 4500–3500 BCE, most likely on the steppes north of the Black and Caspian seas.
description: Comparative linguistics reconstructs Proto-Indo-European, the ancestor of the Indo-European languages now spoken by nearly half of humanity, including inherited words for wheels, wagons, horses and livestock. The steppe or Kurgan hypothesis, developed by Marija Gimbutas, places its speakers among pastoralists of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, from whom the Yamnaya culture spread east and west after about 3300 BCE. Ancient-DNA studies since 2015 have found large-scale steppe-derived ancestry entering Europe and later South Asia, strongly supporting this view, and a 2025 study traced the Yamnaya's ancestry to a population of the Lower Volga and North Caucasus about 4400–4000 BCE. The rival Anatolian hypothesis of Colin Renfrew links the spread of the languages to the first farmers leaving Anatolia around 7000 BCE.
mainstreamView: Most linguists and geneticists now favour a Pontic–Caspian steppe homeland, supported by shared vocabulary for wheeled vehicles invented after about 4000 BCE and by ancient DNA showing large population movements from the steppe. The Anatolian farming hypothesis and variants placing the homeland in Armenia or Iran retain some support, particularly for the origin of the extinct Anatolian branch, so the precise homeland and date remain debated.

title: Austronesian ancestors settle Taiwan
summary: Farmers from coastal southern China settled Taiwan; their descendants later carried Austronesian languages from Madagascar to Easter Island.
description: Linguistic, archaeological and genetic evidence indicates that the Austronesian language family originated in Taiwan, where Neolithic farmers of the Dapenkeng culture, who crossed the Taiwan Strait from the coast of Fujian, are recorded from about 4000–3500 BCE. Taiwan's indigenous languages make up most of the family's primary branches, while all Austronesian languages outside Taiwan belong to a single branch, Malayo-Polynesian. From about 2200 BCE, voyagers in outrigger canoes moved into the Philippines and island Southeast Asia, and their descendants, including the makers of Lapita pottery, eventually settled Remote Oceania from Hawaii to New Zealand and Easter Island and reached Madagascar. This 'Out of Taiwan' model is the majority view, though some scholars emphasise earlier contributions from island Southeast Asia.

title: Horses at Botai: early domestication?
summary: Villagers of the Botai culture in Kazakhstan relied heavily on horses, possibly kept and milked, though their animals were not ancestors of modern horses.
description: Settlements of the Botai culture on the northern Kazakh steppe contain hundreds of thousands of horse bones, and researchers have reported traces of mare's-milk fats in pottery, possible corrals and possible bit wear on teeth, suggesting that horses were penned, milked and perhaps ridden around 3500 BCE. A 2018 genetic study found, however, that the Botai horses were ancestors of Przewalski's horse, previously thought to be a truly wild species, rather than of today's domestic horses. Later genome studies traced modern domestic horses to the lower Volga–Don region around 2200 BCE, from where they spread rapidly across Eurasia. Whether the Botai people domesticated horses or intensively hunted wild herds remains disputed.
mainstreamView: Many archaeologists accept that the Botai people managed or kept horses, based on milk residues, corral traces and dental evidence, but others argue that the finds fit specialised hunting of wild horses, and the bit-wear and milk-residue results have been challenged. It is agreed that the Botai horses did not give rise to modern domestic horses, which originated later on the western steppe.

title: Invention of the wheel
summary: Wheeled vehicles appeared almost simultaneously from Mesopotamia to central Europe; a pot from Bronocice, Poland, bears the oldest known wagon image.
description: The wheel-and-axle combination for transport appears in the archaeological record around 3500 BCE across a wide area from Mesopotamia and the Caucasus to the Pontic steppe and central Europe, so it is unclear where it was first invented. A clay pot from Bronocice in southern Poland, dated to about 3500–3350 BCE, carries what is probably the oldest known depiction of a four-wheeled wagon, while early pictographs from Uruk in Mesopotamia show wheeled vehicles. The oldest surviving wooden wheel with its axle, from the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, is about 5,150 years old. Solid wheels on ox-drawn wagons transformed farming and trade and later warfare, and the earlier potter's wheel, used in Mesopotamia from about 4500–4000 BCE, may have inspired the idea.
